conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having really bad constipation for weeks. It’s worse than ever before. I’ve tried enemas, but only passed a little stool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And any nausea or vomiting with it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been nauseous and not eating much. I’ve also felt really tired, weak, and have had chills for months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. Given your history of diabetes and gastroparesis, this could be related to nerve issues in your gut. We’ll run some tests to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve also been dizzy when I stand up. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We noticed your blood pressure drops when you stand — that’s called orthostatic hypotension. It can be from dehydration or your diabetes affecting nerves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know that had a name. I’ve been so tired I have to sit in the shower.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into that. Your labs show low sodium and elevated creatinine, which suggests dehydration and kidney stress. But your kidney function improved with IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my kidneys failing again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it looks like a temporary issue — prerenal, meaning due to low fluid volume. We’ve stopped your Lasix to help prevent further dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. I’ve been using Zofran for nausea, but I read it can cause constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re switching to Ativan for nausea because Zofran can worsen constipation, especially with your neuropathy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. What about my blood sugar? I haven’t been eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. Your insulin dose was reduced because of poor intake. We’re using a sliding scale to avoid low sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I had a low one this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your glucose was 68. We caught it early. As you start eating again, we’ll adjust your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you some laxatives and an enema. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just had a few bowel movements. My stomach feels much better!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Relieving the constipation should also help with your nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. But I’m still so tired. Is that just from not eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked several things. Your heart function is normal on echo, thyroid is fine, and no infection was found. Your adrenal glands are working too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why am I so tired?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be a mix — your sleep apnea, chronic fatigue, and possibly depression. You’re not using your CPAP, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, the mask doesn’t fit well. I’ve been meaning to get it fixed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve arranged a sleep study and CPAP refit after discharge. That may help your energy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat labs show your sodium is now normal, and creatinine improved to 2.0. That’s your usual baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about the diltiazem? I remember last time we adjusted it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we lowered it to 120 mg daily. It was 360 mg before. This helps reduce swelling and blood pressure without overloading your system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’ve been taking my metoclopramide for gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re keeping that. It helps your stomach empty. But the main issue this time was constipation from neuropathy and Zofran.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, will I need laxatives forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely yes, given your diabetic neuropathy. We’re sending you home with senna, Colace, and Miralax to take daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. And I’ll follow up with my PCP about the fatigue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and with your endocrinologist for diabetes and kidney management. Your glucose has been stable on lower insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your abdomen is no longer tender, and bowel sounds are active. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your new laxatives daily, drink plenty of fluids, wear compression stockings, and sit for 30 seconds before standing to prevent dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I’ll get the CPAP fixed and follow up with my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll see you in follow-up. Take care, and feel better soon.
